# Overview

In Exercise 7, accessibility to eldercare centres was measured from the distances between hexagons
and centres. In this exercise, the distances between villages and stores are used to divide the
residents of Taichung City, Taiwan, among the 28 stores of a fast-food franchise.

On slide 8, the Huff model "estimates the probability of a consumer visiting a specific store by
considering the store's attractiveness and the distance to it, relative to competing stores". The
probabilities define the trade area of each store. Multiplied by the population of each village and
summed over the villages, the probabilities give an estimate of the customers of each store.

**Part 1** is a reproduction of r4gdsa chapter 18, which computes the Huff probabilities with the
`MCI` package, maps the trade area of one store and compares the estimated customers of each store
with its recorded sales. In **Part 2**, the study area, the attraction variable and the distance
exponent of the chapter are checked, the exponent is fitted to the recorded sales, and the trade
areas are mapped as probabilities.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}

## Sources

The hands-on exercise for Lesson 8 is this chapter:

- [Chapter 18: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff
  model](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap18.html)

The Lesson 8 outline lists four readings for before the lesson.

| Reading | What it contributes | Used in |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|----------------------|
| **Rodrigue**, *The Geography of Transport Systems*, A.18 "Spatial Interactions and the Gravity Model" | The general spatial interaction model $T_{ij} = f(V_i, W_j, S_{ij})$, with $S_{ij}$ the "friction of distance" | 3.1 |
| **Rodrigue**, *The Geography of Transport Systems*, A.15 "Market Area Analysis" | Market areas as "ranges of probabilities that customers will attend specific locations (Huff's law)"; the two-store figure of slide 11 | 3.1, 4.4 |
| **Huff (1963)**, "A Probabilistic Analysis of Shopping Center Trade Areas" | The model, with selling space as attraction and travel time as cost; an exponent estimated from data; trade areas as probability contours | 3.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4 |
| **Nakanishi and Cooper (1982)**, "Simplified Estimation Procedures for MCI Models" | Estimation of the MCI model by dummy-variable regression with standard regression packages, from observed market shares | 4 |

Of the eight references the outline also lists, the following is used on this page:

| Reference | What it contributes | Used in |
|----------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|------------------|
| **Wieland (2017)**, "Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations with MCI" | The functions of the `MCI` package; the study area as the first step of a Huff analysis; the fit of $\lambda$ to observed store totals | 3.1, 4.1, 4.3, 4.5 |

The other references are about gravity models of flows between regions (Haynes and Fotheringham,
2020; Farmer and Oshan, 2017; Flowerdew and Aitkin, 1982; Klapka et al., 2013; Yue et al., 2012) and
spatial econometric models of origin-destination flows (Floch and Le Saout, 2018; LeSage and Pace,
2008; Tsutsumi and Tamesue, 2012). Chapter 18 has no flow data, so these references are background
reading for this page. The outline's "All About R" section links `MCI` and `REAT`. `MCI` is used
throughout. `REAT` also has a `huff()` function, which this page does not use.

The Lesson 8 slide deck has 15 slides. Slides 9 and 10 give the utility and the probability of the
Huff model. Slides 12 and 13 give the expected customers and the market share of each store. Slides
14 and 15 give the MCI model.

:::

# Getting started

## Packages

```{r}
pacman::p_load(sf, MCI, tmap, ggstatsplot,
               patchwork, knitr, tidyverse)
tmap_options(component.autoscale = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
pacman::p_load(...)                                       # pacman
tmap_options(component.autoscale)                         # tmap
```

- `p_load()` loads each package, and installs any that are missing.
- `tmap_options(component.autoscale = FALSE)` stops `tmap` from shrinking the titles, legends and
  scale bars of the maps when they do not fit.

| Package | Used for |
|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `sf` | reading the shapefiles, points inside the villages, distances |
| `MCI` | `huff.shares()`, `shares.total()` and `huff.lambda()` |
| `tmap` | maps |
| `ggstatsplot` | the scatter plot with a correlation test in section 3.6 |
| `patchwork` | placing two charts side by side |
| `knitr` | tables |
| `tidyverse` | reading, joining and reshaping the tables (`readr`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`), and `ggplot2` charts |
:::

## The data

The data sets are distributed with the exercise on eLearn, in the folder `data/`.

| Data set | Format | Features | Contents |
|-------------------------|--------------|------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| `STORES_TC` | ESRI shapefile | 28 points | stores of the franchise in Taichung City, with name, address and store code |
| `TOWN_TC` | ESRI shapefile | 28 polygons | districts of Taichung City |
| `VILLAGE_TC` | ESRI shapefile | 622 polygons | villages (里) of Taichung City, with the village code `VILLCODE` |
| `pop2019.csv` | CSV | 625 rows | households (`H_CNT`), population (`P_CNT`), males (`M_CNT`) and females (`F_CNT`) of each village, December 2019 |
| `Store_sales_data.csv` | CSV | 5,499 rows | number of bills and sales amount (currency not given) by store code and `POD code` |

The folder also has `storeCD.csv` and a second store layer, `STORES_TC1`, which the chapter does not
use. `storeCD.csv` gives each of the 28 stores the same `Capacity`, 50, with no unit. `STORES_TC1`
has the 28 stores and a 29th point, "New Store", with the code `NS`.

## Geospatial data

### Reading the three layers

```{r}
#| results: hide
stores <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                  layer = "STORES_TC")
town <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                layer = "TOWN_TC")
village <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                   layer = "VILLAGE_TC")
```

```{r}
tibble(layer = c("stores", "town", "village"),
       features = c(nrow(stores), nrow(town), nrow(village)),
       geometry = c(as.character(st_geometry_type(stores, by_geometry = FALSE)),
                    as.character(st_geometry_type(town, by_geometry = FALSE)),
                    as.character(st_geometry_type(village, by_geometry = FALSE))),
       epsg = c(st_crs(stores)$epsg, st_crs(town)$epsg, st_crs(village)$epsg)) |>
  kable()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
st_read(dsn, layer)                                       # sf
st_geometry_type(x, by_geometry = FALSE)                  # sf
st_crs(x)$epsg                                            # sf
tibble(...)                                               # tibble
kable(x, digits)                                          # knitr
```

- `st_read()` reads the shapefile named by `layer` from the folder `dsn` into a simple feature data
  frame. `results: hide` suppresses the report that `st_read()` prints for each file.
- `st_geometry_type(by_geometry = FALSE)` returns one geometry type for the whole layer.
- `st_crs()$epsg` returns the EPSG code of the coordinate reference system.
- `tibble()` builds a data frame with one row for each layer, and `kable()` prints it as a table.
  The other tables on this page are also printed with `kable()`. Where `digits` is given, it rounds
  the numbers.
:::

The three layers are in TWD97 / TM2 zone 121, EPSG:3826, a projected coordinate system in metres, so
distances between the layers can be computed without a transformation.

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: layers-map
#| eval: false
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
str_remove(string, pattern); recode(x, old = new)         # stringr, dplyr
st_make_grid(x, cellsize, what = "centers")               # sf
st_distance(x, y); st_cast(x, "MULTILINESTRING")          # sf
st_bbox(x); st_as_sfc(bbox); st_buffer(x, dist)           # sf
st_crop(x, bbox); st_difference(x, y)                     # sf
tm_shape(shp, bbox) + tm_polygons(fill, col, lwd)         # tmap
tm_borders(col, lwd, lty); tm_dots(fill, size)            # tmap
tm_text(text, size, col, fontface, ymod)                  # tmap
tm_add_legend(type, labels, fill, col, lty)               # tmap
tm_compass(); tm_scalebar(); tm_grid()                    # tmap
```

- `TOWNENG` holds the English name of each district, such as "Xitun District". `str_remove()` drops
  " District", and `recode()` writes out the short names of the five central districts, such as "W."
  for West and "Zhong" for Central.
- The five central districts cover 0.9 to 7.8 km² each, too small for a name on the map of the whole
  city. The dashed rectangle marks them on the first map, and the second map shows them at a larger
  scale.
- `label_point()` finds a place for the name of a district. `st_make_grid()` puts points 250 m apart
  over the district, and the function keeps the point farthest from both the district boundary and
  the nearest store, so that the name lies inside its district and clear of the store labels.
- For the second map, `st_crop()` cuts the districts to the rectangle, `st_difference()` removes 400
  m around each store, and `st_point_on_surface()` places each name in the area that remains.
  `bbox = zoom` in the first `tm_shape()` sets the extent of the map to the rectangle.
- Each `tm_shape()` starts a layer, and the layers are drawn in order: the villages in grey, the
  district boundaries in blue, the district names in blue italics, and the stores as red points.
- `tm_text()` writes the store code of each point. `ymod` moves the label up so that it does not
  cover the point.
- Each layer is drawn in one colour, so `tm_add_legend()` adds one legend entry for each layer.
- `tm_compass()`, `tm_scalebar()` and `tm_grid()` add a north arrow, a scale bar and grid lines with
  coordinates in metres. `legend.outside = TRUE` places the legend outside the map frame: to the
  right of the map, or below it when the legend is too wide for the space on the right.
:::
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
store_town <- st_join(stores, town) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(TOWNNAME)
```

The 28 stores are in `r nrow(store_town)` of the `r nrow(town)` districts of the town layer. Xitun
District (西屯區) has `r store_town$n[store_town$TOWNNAME == "西屯區"]` stores, the most of any district.
Six stores are in the five central districts: DT and TY in North District, MT in West District, FH
and GS in South District, and JW in East District.

```{r}
store_sales <- read_csv("data/aspatial/Store_sales_data.csv")
```

### Store sales

```{r}
summary(store_sales)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
n_codes <- n_distinct(store_sales$`Store Code`, na.rm = TRUE)
n_tc_rows <- sum(store_sales$`Store Code` %in% stores$Store_CD)
n_na_code <- sum(is.na(store_sales$`Store Code`))
```

The file has `r format(nrow(store_sales), big.mark = ",")` rows for `r n_codes` store codes. Of
these rows, `r n_na_code` have no store code. Of the rows, `r n_tc_rows` belong to the 28 stores in
Taichung. The other store codes are not in `STORES_TC` and drop out at the join in section 2.5.2.
Each row gives the number of bills and the sales amount of one store for one `POD code`. The data
come with no description of the `POD code`, the currency of the amounts or the period of the sales.

## Data preparation

### Aggregating store sales

```{r}
store_sales_aggre <- store_sales |>
  group_by(`Store Code`) |>
  summarise(Total_Bill = sum(Bills, na.rm = TRUE),
            Total_Sales = sum(Amount, na.rm = TRUE))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
group_by(x, ...); summarise(...)                          # dplyr
```

- `group_by()` groups the rows by store code, and `summarise()` returns one row for each store code,
  with the sum of the bills and the sum of the sales amount over all its `POD code` rows.
- The backticks around `` `Store Code` `` are needed because the column name contains a space.
:::

### Relational join

```{r}
stores <- stores |>
  left_join(store_sales_aggre,
            by = join_by(Store_CD == `Store Code`)) |>
  mutate(Store_size = 100)

summary(stores)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
left_join(x, y, by = join_by(a == b))                     # dplyr
mutate(Store_size = 100)                                  # dplyr
```

- `left_join()` keeps the 28 rows of `stores` and adds the total bills and sales of the row of
  `store_sales_aggre` whose `Store Code` equals the store's `Store_CD`. The rows of
  `store_sales_aggre` with store codes that are not in `stores` are dropped.
- `mutate()` adds the column `Store_size` with the value 100 for every store, the value of the
  chapter. `Store_size` is the attraction of the store in the Huff model of Part 1.
:::

The summary has no missing values in `Total_Bill` and `Total_Sales`, so each of the 28 stores has
sales records. In the currency of the file, which is not given, the total sales range
from `r format(min(stores$Total_Sales), big.mark = ",")` for
store `r stores$Store_CD[which.min(stores$Total_Sales)]`
to `r format(max(stores$Total_Sales), big.mark = ",")` for
store `r stores$Store_CD[which.max(stores$Total_Sales)]`.

### Tidying the population table

```{r}
glimpse(pop2019)
```

```{r}
glimpse(village)
```

The village code `V_ID` of `pop2019` has a hyphen after the district code, as in `66000110-002`. The
code `VILLCODE` of `village` has the same digits without the hyphen.

```{r}
pop2019 <- pop2019 |>
  mutate(V_ID = str_remove_all(V_ID, "-"))

village <- village |>
  left_join(pop2019,
            by = join_by(VILLCODE == V_ID))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
str_remove_all(string, pattern)                           # stringr
```

- `str_remove_all()` deletes every hyphen from `V_ID`, so that `66000110-002` becomes `66000110002`,
  the form of `VILLCODE`.
- `left_join()` keeps the 622 polygons of `village` and adds the population columns of the row of
  `pop2019` with the same code.
:::

# Part 1: Chapter 18

## The Huff model

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## The model of Huff (1963)

In "Spatial Interactions and the Gravity Model", section A.18 of the Methods chapter of *The
Geography of Transport Systems*, Rodrigue writes the general spatial interaction model as

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{ij} &= f(V_i, W_j, S_{ij}) \\
&= f(\text{attributes of origin } i, \ \text{attributes of destination } j, \ \text{friction of distance from } i \text{ to } j)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $T_{ij}$ is the interaction between origin $i$ and destination $j$. Slide 7 gives the same
model. In the Huff model, the attribute of the destination is the attraction of a store and the
friction is the distance to it.

**Reilly's law: the retail model of slide 7.** The third model of slide 7 gives the breaking point
between two centres:

$$
\begin{aligned}
B_{ij} &= \frac{S_{ij}}{1 + W_j / V_i} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{\text{distance between centres } i \text{ and } j}{1 + \text{size of } j \div \text{size of } i}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $B_{ij}$ is the distance from centre $i$ to the breaking point. In the example of the slide,
centres $i$ of size 35 and $j$ of size 15 are 7 units apart, and the breaking point is $7 / (1 +
15/35) = 4.9$ units from $i$, nearer the smaller centre $j$.

Huff (1963, p. 82) traces the breaking point to the "Law of Retail Gravitation" of Reilly (1929): a
town between two cities divides its trade between them "in direct proportion to the populations of
the two cities and in inverse proportion to the square of the distances". In the notation of Huff,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{B_a}{B_b} &= \frac{P_a}{P_b} \left(\frac{D_b}{D_a}\right)^2 \\[4pt]
&= \frac{\text{population of city } a}{\text{population of city } b} \times \left(\frac{\text{distance from the town to city } b}{\text{distance from the town to city } a}\right)^2
\end{aligned}
$$

where $B_a$ and $B_b$ are the proportions of the trade of the town attracted by cities $a$ and $b$.
The breaking point is the town where $B_a = B_b$, which Huff calls "the .5 probability position
between two cities". With the squared distance, the breaking point lies $D_{ab} / (1 + \sqrt{P_a /
P_b})$ from city $b$, where $D_{ab}$ is the distance between the two cities. The retail model of
slide 7 has no square root: it divides by the distance itself, as the figure of slide 11 does.
Rodrigue (A.15) lists Reilly's law as the step at which "market size" entered market area analysis.
Wieland (2017, p. 298) calls these early models deterministic: "each customer origin is assigned
completely to one supply location".

In the Huff model, the ratio of Reilly is extended to any number of stores, with a probability for
each store. With two stores and $\lambda = 2$, the ratio $p_{ia} / p_{ib}$ of the Huff model below
is the ratio $B_a / B_b$ of Reilly.

Huff (1963, p. 86) gives the probability that consumers in statistical unit $i$ travel to shopping
centre $j$ as the selling space of $j$ divided by a power of the travel time from $i$ to $j$,
relative to the same ratio for every centre. On slides 9 and 10, in the notation of Wieland (2017,
p. 299), the utility of store $j$ for the customers of origin $i$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
U_{ij} &= A_j^{\gamma} \, d_{ij}^{-\lambda} \\
&= \frac{(\text{attraction of store } j)^{\gamma}}{(\text{distance from village } i \text{ to store } j)^{\lambda}}
\end{aligned}
$$

and the probability that the customers of $i$ choose $j$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{ij} &= \frac{U_{ij}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n} U_{ik}} = \frac{A_j^{\gamma} \, d_{ij}^{-\lambda}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n} A_k^{\gamma} \, d_{ik}^{-\lambda}} \\[6pt]
&= \frac{(\text{attraction of store } j)^{\gamma} \div (\text{distance from village } i \text{ to store } j)^{\lambda}}{\text{sum over all } n \text{ stores } k \text{ of } (\text{attraction of store } k)^{\gamma} \div (\text{distance from village } i \text{ to store } k)^{\lambda}}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $A_j$ is the attraction of store $j$, $d_{ij}$ is the distance or travel time, $\gamma$ is the
weight of the attraction and $\lambda$ is the weight of the distance. The probabilities of one
origin sum to 1.

On slide 12, the expected number of customers from $i$ at $j$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{ij} &= p_{ij} \, C_i \\
&= (\text{probability of store } j \text{ for village } i) \times (\text{market potential of village } i)
\end{aligned}
$$

where the market potential $C_i$ is the number of potential customers or the purchasing power in
village $i$. On slide 13, the expected customers of store $j$ in the whole study area and the market
share of store $j$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_j &= \sum_{i} E_{ij} \\
&= \text{sum over all villages } i \text{ of the expected customers from } i \text{ at store } j
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_j &= \frac{T_j}{\sum_{k=1}^{n} T_k} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{\text{expected customers of store } j}{\text{expected customers of all } n \text{ stores}}
\end{aligned}
$$

The symbols of the formulas, and the columns that hold them in the code of this page:

| Symbol | Meaning | Column |
|------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------|
| $i$ | origin: a village | `VILLCODE` |
| $j$, $k$ | a store | `Store_CD` |
| $n$ | number of stores: 28 | |
| $A_j$ | attraction of store $j$ | `Store_size` |
| $d_{ij}$ | distance from village $i$ to store $j$, in metres | `distance` |
| $\gamma$, $\lambda$ | weights of the attraction and the distance | arguments `gamma` and `lambda` |
| $U_{ij}$ | utility of store $j$ for the residents of village $i$ | `U_ij` |
| $p_{ij}$ | probability that a resident of village $i$ chooses store $j$ | `p_ij` |
| $C_i$ | market potential of village $i$: its residents | `P_CNT` |
| $E_{ij}$ | expected customers from village $i$ at store $j$ | computed in `shares.total()` |
| $T_j$ | expected customers of store $j$ | `sum_E_j` |
| $M_j$ | market share of store $j$ | `share_j` |
| $S_j$ | recorded sales of store $j$, rescaled to persons (section 4.3) | `sales_scaled` |

`huff.shares()` of the `MCI` package writes the decay as $d_{ij}^{\lambda}$ with a negative
`lambda`. Its default `lambda = -2` corresponds to $\lambda = 2$ in the formula above.

**Example: one village and two stores.** Panel 1 uses the numbers of the figure on slide 11, which
comes from "Market Area Analysis" (Rodrigue, A.15): a village halfway between store a, of size
250,000, and store b, of size 100,000, with the two stores 75 km apart. Panel 2 gives the two stores
the same size and moves the village to 25 km from store a. The figure uses $\gamma = 1$ and $\lambda
= 2$, the defaults of `huff.shares()`.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7.2
#| out-width: "100%"
hf_panel <- function(title, size_a, size_b, d_a) {
  hf <- tibble(store = c("a", "b"), x = c(0, 75), size = c(size_a, size_b),
               d = c(d_a, 75 - d_a)) |>
    mutate(U = size / d^2,
           p = U / sum(U),
           U_lab = sprintf("%s ÷ %g² = %.0f", scales::comma(size), d, U))
  hex <- tibble(t = seq(0, 300, by = 60) * pi / 180,
                x = d_a + 2.6 * cos(t), y = 0.23 * sin(t))
  bar <- tibble(xmin = d_a - 18 + c(0, 36 * hf$p[1]), xmax = d_a - 18 + c(36 * hf$p[1], 36))
  ggplot() +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -17, xmax = 92, ymin = -1.95, ymax = 2.55, fill = "white",
             colour = "grey65") +
    annotate("text", x = -15, y = 2.42, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, fontface = "bold", size = 4.3,
             label = title) +
    annotate("text", x = -15, y = 2.1, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 3.8, colour = "grey25",
             label = "utility = size ÷ distance², with distance in km") +
    annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 75, y = 0, yend = 0, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 1) +
    annotate("segment", x = c(5, d_a + 3.5), xend = c(d_a - 3.5, 70), y = 0.55, yend = 0.55,
             colour = "grey40", arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.08, "in"))) +
    annotate("text", x = c(d_a / 2 + 0.75, (d_a + 75) / 2 - 0.75), y = 0.8,
             label = paste(hf$d, "km"), size = 4) +
    geom_rect(data = bar, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = 1.25, ymax = 1.65),
              fill = c("#3182bd", "#9ecae1"), colour = "white") +
    annotate("text", x = c((bar$xmin[1] + bar$xmax[1]) / 2, bar$xmax[2] + 1.5), y = 1.45,
             hjust = c(0.5, 0), size = 4, colour = c("white", "black"),
             label = sprintf("%s %.2f", hf$store, hf$p)) +
    annotate("text", x = d_a, y = 1.82, size = 3.8, colour = "grey25",
             label = "share of the village's customers") +
    geom_point(data = hf, aes(x, 0, size = size, fill = store), shape = 21, colour = "grey30") +
    geom_text(data = hf, aes(x, 0, label = store), size = 4.5, fontface = "bold",
              colour = c("white", "black")) +
    geom_polygon(data = hex, aes(x, y), fill = "#a1d99b", colour = "grey30") +
    annotate("text", x = d_a, y = -0.45, label = "village", size = 3.8) +
    geom_text(data = hf, aes(x, -0.75, label = paste("store", store, "\nsize", scales::comma(size))),
              size = 3.8, lineheight = 0.9) +
    geom_text(data = hf, aes(x, -1.3, label = paste("utility", U_lab)), size = 3.8, colour = "grey25") +
    annotate("text", x = -15, y = -1.72, hjust = 0, size = 3.8, colour = "grey25",
             label = sprintf("share of a = %.0f ÷ (%.0f + %.0f) = %.2f,   share of b = %.0f ÷ %.0f = %.2f",
                             hf$U[1], hf$U[1], hf$U[2], hf$p[1],
                             hf$U[2], sum(hf$U), hf$p[2])) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(a = "#3182bd", b = "#9ecae1"), guide = "none") +
    scale_size_area(max_size = 19, limits = c(0, 250000), guide = "none") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-17, 92), ylim = c(-1.95, 2.55), expand = FALSE) +
    theme_void()
}

hf_panel("1. Village halfway, store a 2.5 times as large", 250000, 100000, 37.5) /
  hf_panel("2. Stores of the same size, village closer to a", 100000, 100000, 25)
```

In panel 1, the two distances are equal, so $37.5^2$ cancels from the fraction and the shares are in
the ratio of the sizes: $250{,}000 \div 350{,}000 = 0.71$. Rodrigue's figure divides by the distance
itself ($\lambda = 1$) and gives the same 0.71, because the exponent has no effect when the two
distances are equal. In panel 2, the two sizes are equal, so the size cancels and the shares depend
on the distances only: store a, at half the distance of store b, has four times the utility of store
b. Every store in chapter 18 has the same size (section 4.2), so the model of Part 1 works as in
panel 2.
:::

## Distance matrix

```{r}
village_center <- st_point_on_surface(village)
distmat <- st_distance(village_center, stores)

dim(distmat)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
st_point_on_surface(x)                                    # sf
st_distance(x, y)                                         # sf
```

- `st_point_on_surface()` returns one point for each village, always inside the polygon. For a
  village with a concave or multi-part shape, the centroid can be outside the polygon.
- `st_distance()` returns a matrix of straight-line distances in metres, with one row for each
  village point and one column for each store.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
gap_m <- as.numeric(st_distance(village_center, st_centroid(village),
                                by_element = TRUE))
n_outside <- sum(!diag(st_intersects(st_centroid(village), village, sparse = FALSE)))
gap_yongan <- gap_m[village$VILLCODE == "66000060018"]
```

In the text of chapter 18, the village points are called centroids. The median distance between the
point on the surface and the centroid of a village is `r round(median(gap_m))` m. The largest
distance is `r format(round(max(gap_m)), big.mark = ",")` m. In `r n_outside` villages, the centroid
lies outside the village. The map below shows one of them, Yong'an Village (永安里) in Xitun District,
where the two points are `r round(gap_yongan)` m apart.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Map

```{r}
#| label: centroid-map
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5.5
dm_v <- filter(village, VILLCODE == "66000060018")
dm_pts <- st_sf(point = c("centroid", "point on the surface"),
                geometry = c(st_geometry(st_centroid(dm_v)),
                             st_geometry(st_point_on_surface(dm_v))))
dm_box <- st_bbox(st_buffer(dm_v, 600))

tm_shape(village, bbox = dm_box) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey75", lwd = 0.5) +
tm_shape(dm_v) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "#a1d99b", col = "grey20", lwd = 1.5) +
tm_shape(dm_pts) +
  tm_symbols(shape = "point", fill = "point", size = 1.2, col = "grey20",
             fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = c("#e6550d", "#3182bd")),
             shape.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = c(4, 21)),
             fill.legend = tm_legend(title = ""), shape.legend = tm_legend_combine("fill")) +
  tm_add_legend(type = "polygons", labels = "village Yong'an", fill = "#a1d99b",
                col = "grey20") +

  tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom")) +

```

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: centroid-map
#| eval: false
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
st_centroid(x); st_point_on_surface(x)                    # sf
tm_symbols(shape, fill, size, fill.scale, shape.scale)    # tmap
tm_scale_categorical(values); tm_legend_combine(x)        # tmap
```

- `dm_pts` holds the two points of Yong'an Village: its centroid and its point on the surface.
- `bbox` in the first `tm_shape()` sets the extent of the map to the village with a margin of 600 m.
- `tm_symbols()` draws the centroid as a cross and the point on the surface as a blue circle.
  `tm_legend_combine("fill")` puts the shape and the colour of each point in one legend entry.
:::
:::

The centroid is the centre of mass of the polygon. Yong'an Village is a narrow strip to the west and
a wider block to the east, and the centre of mass of the two falls between them, outside the
village. `st_point_on_surface()` returns a point inside the polygon.

Each row of `distmat` holds the distances from one village to the 28 stores. The map below shows the
row of Pingxin Village (平心里) in Beitun District, the village in which store BT is located.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Map

```{r}
tm_shape(village) +
```

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: distance-row-map
#| eval: false
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
st_nearest_points(x, y)                                   # sf
tm_lines(col, lwd, col.scale, col.legend)                 # tmap
tm_scale_intervals(breaks, labels, values)                # tmap
```

- `dm_k` is the row number of Pingxin Village in `village` and in `distmat`.
- `st_nearest_points()` returns a straight line from the village point to each store. `dm_lines`
  holds the 28 lines with the distances of row `dm_k` of `distmat` in kilometres.
- `tm_lines()` colours each line by its distance class. `tm_scale_intervals()` sets the class breaks
  at 2, 5, 10 and 15 km.
:::
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
dm_row <- arrange(st_drop_geometry(dm_lines), distance_km)
```

The distances in the row of Pingxin Village run from `r round(dm_row$distance_km[1], 1)` km to
store `r dm_row$Store_CD[1]` to `r round(dm_row$distance_km[28], 1)` km to
store `r dm_row$Store_CD[28]`. Each of the `r nrow(village)` rows of `distmat` holds 28 distances in
the same way.

```{r}
rownames(distmat) <- village$VILLCODE
colnames(distmat) <- stores$Store_CD

distmat_long <- distmat |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "VILLCODE") |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -VILLCODE,
               names_to = "Store_CD",
               values_to = "distance") |>
  mutate(distance = as.numeric(distance))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
rownames(x) <- ...; colnames(x) <- ...                    # base R
rownames_to_column(df, var)                               # tibble
pivot_longer(df, cols, names_to, values_to)               # tidyr
```

- `rownames()` and `colnames()` set the village codes as the row names of the matrix and the store
  codes as its column names.
- `as.data.frame()` turns the matrix into a data frame with one column for each store, and
  `rownames_to_column()` moves the row names into a column `VILLCODE`.
- `pivot_longer()` turns the 28 store columns into rows: one row for each pair of village and store,
  with the store code in `Store_CD` and the distance in `distance`.
- `as.numeric()` removes the unit "m" that `st_distance()` attaches to the distances.
:::

In `distmat`, each row is a village $i$, each column is a store $j$, and each cell holds the
distance $d_{ij}$ in metres. The table below shows the first three rows and the first four columns.

```{r}
#| echo: false
show_rows <- function(df, rows) {
  out <- df[rows, , drop = FALSE] |>
    mutate(across(everything(), as.character)) |>
    mutate(row = format(rows, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), .before = 1)
  gap <- out[1, ]
  gap[1, ] <- as.list(rep("...", ncol(out)))
  breaks <- c(which(diff(rows) > 1), if (max(rows) < nrow(df)) length(rows))
  for (g in rev(breaks)) out <- bind_rows(out[seq_len(g), ], gap, out[-seq_len(g), ])
  out
}
comma0 <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)

dm_corner <- distmat[1:3, 1:4] |>
  units::drop_units() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(across(everything(), comma0)) |>
  rownames_to_column("village $i$")
bind_rows(dm_corner, as.list(set_names(rep("...", 5), names(dm_corner)))) |>
  mutate(`...` = "...") |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrr")
```

`pivot_longer()` turns each cell of `distmat` into a row of `distmat_long`. The four cells of the
first row of `distmat` become rows 1 to 4:

```{r}
#| echo: false
distmat_long |>
  mutate(distance = comma0(distance)) |>
  show_rows(1:4) |>
  kable(col.names = c("row", "village $i$<br>`VILLCODE`", "store $j$<br>`Store_CD`",
                      "distance $d_{ij}$ (m)<br>`distance`"),
        align = "lllr")
```

## Interaction matrix

`huff.shares()` takes one table, the interaction matrix of Wieland (2017, p. 300), with one row for
each pair of origin and store and the columns for the attraction and the distance.

```{r}
interaction_matrix <- distmat_long |>
  left_join(stores |>
              st_drop_geometry() |>
              select(Store_CD, Store_size),
            by = "Store_CD") |>
  relocate(distance, .after = last_col())

summary(interaction_matrix)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
select(df, ...); relocate(df, x, .after = last_col())     # dplyr
```

- The join adds the `Store_size` of each store to its rows. `st_drop_geometry()` removes the store
  points first, so that the result is a plain data frame.
- `relocate()` moves `distance` to the last column. The column order does not matter to
  `huff.shares()`, which finds the columns by name.
:::

The matrix has `r format(nrow(interaction_matrix), big.mark = ",")` rows, one for each of
the `r nrow(village)` villages paired with each of the 28 stores. The shortest distance
is `r round(min(interaction_matrix$distance))` m, and the longest distance
is `r format(round(max(interaction_matrix$distance) / 1000, 1), nsmall = 1)` km.

The rows are ordered by village. Rows 1 to 28 pair the first village, Jianxing Village (建興里) in
Dajia District, with each of the 28 stores, and row 29 starts the second village. The table below
shows six of the rows.

```{r}
#| echo: false
interaction_matrix |>
  mutate(Store_size = as.character(Store_size),
         distance = comma0(distance)) |>
  show_rows(c(1:3, 28, 29, nrow(interaction_matrix))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("row", "village $i$<br>`VILLCODE`", "store $j$<br>`Store_CD`",
                      "attraction $A_j$<br>`Store_size`",
                      "distance $d_{ij}$ (m)<br>`distance`"),
        align = "lllrr")
```

Each row holds one pair of village and store, with the two inputs of the utility $U_{ij}$ of section
3.1: the attraction $A_j$ and the distance $d_{ij}$. `huff.shares()` computes one probability
$p_{ij}$ for each row.

## Huff probabilities

```{r}
huff_share <- huff.shares(interaction_matrix,
                          "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
                          "Store_size", "distance")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
huff.shares(huffdataset, origins, locations, attrac, dist,
            gamma = 1, lambda = -2)                       # MCI
```

- The arguments name the columns of the interaction matrix: origins, locations, attraction and
  distance.
- With the defaults `gamma = 1` and `lambda = -2`, `huff.shares()` computes $U_{ij} = A_j \,
  d_{ij}^{-2}$ for each row and writes it to `U_ij`. It writes the sum of $U_{ij}$ over the 28
  stores of each village to `sum_U_ij`, and the probability $p_{ij}$ to `p_ij`.
:::

```{r}
huff_share |>
  group_by(VILLCODE) |>
  summarise(sum_p = sum(p_ij)) |>
  pull(sum_p) |>
  range()
```

The probabilities of each village sum to 1, as in the formula of section 3.1.

`huff_share` is the interaction matrix with three new columns. `huff.shares()` also sorts the rows
by village code and store code, so the first village of `huff_share` is Jiguang Village (繼光里) in
Central District, and its first store is BT. The table below shows five of the rows.

```{r}
#| echo: false
huff_share |>
  mutate(distance = comma0(distance),
         U_ij = formatC(U_ij, format = "e", digits = 2),
         sum_U_ij = formatC(unlist(sum_U_ij), format = "e", digits = 2),
         p_ij = formatC(p_ij, format = "f", digits = 3)) |>
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, distance, U_ij, sum_U_ij, p_ij) |>
  show_rows(c(1:3, 28, 29)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("row", "village $i$<br>`VILLCODE`", "store $j$<br>`Store_CD`",
                      "distance $d_{ij}$ (m)<br>`distance`", "utility $U_{ij}$<br>`U_ij`",
                      "sum of utilities $\\sum_k U_{ik}$<br>`sum_U_ij`",
                      "probability $p_{ij}$<br>`p_ij`"),
        align = "lllrrrr")
```

In row 1, $U_{ij} = 100 \times 3{,}807^{-2} = 6.90 \times 10^{-6}$ and $p_{ij} = 6.90 \times 10^{-6}
\div 1.97 \times 10^{-4} = 0.035$. `sum_U_ij` is the same in the 28 rows of a village.
`huff.shares()` stores `sum_U_ij` as a list column, so `unlist()` turns it into numbers for the
table. `Store_size` is left out of the table: it is 100 in every row.

## Trade area of store BT

```{r}
market_share <- huff_share |>
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")

Trade_area <- village |>
  left_join(market_share, by = "VILLCODE")

selected_store <- stores |>
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `filter()` keeps the `r nrow(village)` rows of store BT, one for each village.
- `left_join()` adds the probability `p_ij` of store BT to each village polygon. The chapter's
  `left_join()` has no `by` and joins on `VILLCODE`, the one column the two tables share. Here the
  key is written out.
- `selected_store` is the point of store BT, drawn on the map.
:::

`Trade_area` holds the `r nrow(Trade_area)` village polygons, each with the distance to store BT and
the probability of choosing BT. The table below shows six of its `r ncol(Trade_area)` columns for
the first three villages.

```{r}
#| echo: false
Trade_area |>
  mutate(geometry_type = as.character(st_geometry_type(Trade_area))) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(distance = comma0(distance),
         p_ij = formatC(p_ij, format = "f", digits = 3)) |>
  select(VILLCODE, VILLENG, Store_CD, distance, p_ij, geometry_type) |>
  show_rows(1:3) |>
  kable(col.names = c("row", "village $i$<br>`VILLCODE`", "village name<br>`VILLENG`", "store $j$<br>`Store_CD`",
                      "distance $d_{ij}$ (m)<br>`distance`", "probability $p_{ij}$<br>`p_ij`",
                      "polygon<br>`geometry`"),
        align = "llllrrl")
```


::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 10, values)    # tmap
```

- `tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 10)`, the setting of the chapter, divides the villages
  into ten classes of equal size, the deciles of `p_ij`, and colours them from light to dark blue.
- The store is drawn as a red point with a black outline.
:::
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
bt_dec <- quantile(Trade_area$p_ij, c(0.5, 0.9))
bt_ctx <- huff_share |>
  group_by(VILLCODE) |>
  summarise(p_bt = p_ij[Store_CD == "BT"],
            d_bt = distance[Store_CD == "BT"] / 1000,
            d_other = min(distance[Store_CD != "BT"]) / 1000) |>
  mutate(decile = ntile(p_bt, 10))
bt_d1 <- bt_ctx |> filter(decile == 1)
bt_d57 <- bt_ctx |> filter(decile %in% 5:7)
```

The probability of choosing BT is highest in the villages around the store. The median village has a
probability of `r round(bt_dec[1], 3)`. The darkest class, the top decile, spans the probabilities
from `r round(bt_dec[2], 3)` to `r round(max(Trade_area$p_ij), 3)`, a range
about `r round((max(Trade_area$p_ij) - bt_dec[2]) / bt_dec[2])` times as wide as that of the
lightest nine classes together.

The probability also depends on the distance to the other stores. In the lowest decile, the median
distance to BT is `r round(median(bt_d1$d_bt), 1)` km and the median distance to the nearest other
store is `r round(median(bt_d1$d_other), 2)` km. In deciles 5 to 7, the median distance to BT is
similar, `r round(median(bt_d57$d_bt), 1)` km. The nearest other store of these villages is a median
of `r round(median(bt_d57$d_other), 1)` km away, so the other stores add less utility to the
denominator of $p_{ij}$, and the probability of choosing BT is higher.

## Estimated customers of each store

On slide 12, the expected customers from village $i$ at store $j$ are $E_{ij} = p_{ij} C_i$. In the
chapter, $C_i$ is the population of the village, `P_CNT`.

```{r}
huff_share_pp <- huff_share |>
  left_join(village |>
              st_drop_geometry() |>
              select(VILLCODE, P_CNT),
            by = "VILLCODE") |>
  relocate(distance, .after = last_col())

huff_total <- shares.total(huff_share_pp,
                           "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
                           "p_ij", "P_CNT")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
shares.total(mcidataset, submarkets, suppliers,
             shares, localmarket)                         # MCI
```

- The join adds the population of each village to its 28 rows.
- `shares.total()` multiplies each probability by the population of its village and sums the
  products over the villages of each store. It returns one row for each store, with the store code
  in `suppliers_single`, the estimated customers $T_j$ in `sum_E_j` and the market share in
  `share_j`.
:::

`huff_share_pp` adds the population `P_CNT` of each village to `huff_share`. The expected customers
$E_{ij}$ are computed inside `shares.total()` and are not a column of `huff_share_pp`. The last
column of the table below computes them for the first three rows.

```{r}
#| echo: false
huff_share_pp |>
  mutate(E_ij = comma0(p_ij * P_CNT),
         p_ij = formatC(p_ij, format = "f", digits = 3),
         P_CNT = comma0(P_CNT)) |>
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, p_ij, P_CNT, E_ij) |>
  show_rows(1:3) |>
  kable(col.names = c("row", "village $i$<br>`VILLCODE`", "store $j$<br>`Store_CD`", "probability $p_{ij}$<br>`p_ij`",
                      "residents $C_i$<br>`P_CNT`",
                      "expected customers $E_{ij} = p_{ij} C_i$<br>(computed for this table)"),
        align = "lllrrr")
```

`huff_total` has one row for each store:

```{r}
#| echo: false
huff_total |>
  mutate(sum_E_j = comma0(sum_E_j),
         share_j = formatC(share_j, format = "f", digits = 4)) |>
  show_rows(c(1:3, 28)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("row", "store $j$<br>`suppliers_single`",
                      "expected customers $T_j$<br>`sum_E_j`", "market share $M_j$<br>`share_j`"),
        align = "llrr")
```

```{r}
store_sales_est <- stores |>
  left_join(huff_total,
            by = join_by(Store_CD == suppliers_single)) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
```

The sum of `sum_E_j` over the 28 stores
is `r format(round(sum(store_sales_est$sum_E_j)), big.mark = ",")`, the population of
the `r nrow(village)` villages. The residents of each village are divided among the 28 stores by the
probabilities $p_{ij}$, which sum to 1. The chart compares the estimated customers with the recorded
sales of each store. In the "How to read" tab, the same chart carries a note on each of its parts: the dots, the fitted
line and its band, the line of results, the two histograms on the margins and their count scale.

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
ggscatterstats(data, x, y, xlab, ylab, bf.message)        # ggstatsplot
theme(text, plot.subtitle, ggside.axis.text)              # ggplot2, ggside
```

- `ggscatterstats()` draws one point for each store, a least-squares line with its confidence band,
  and the result of a Pearson correlation test in the subtitle.
- By default, `ggscatterstats()` also draws histograms on the top and right margins: the estimated
  customers of the 28 stores along the top, and their recorded sales along the right side. Each bar counts the
  stores in one bin.
- `bf.message = FALSE` leaves out the second line of results, printed below the chart in the
  chapter's call. That line is a Bayesian version of the test. The lessons use p-values, so only the
  frequentist line of results is shown.
- `theme(text = element_text(size = 13))` enlarges the axis labels and titles, and `plot.subtitle`
  sets the size of the line of results. The `ggside` package draws the histograms on the margins.
  `ggside.axis.text` sets their count labels to 8 points so that the labels 0 to 4 do not overlap.
- `ggscatterstats()` returns a `ggplot2` chart, so `scale_x_continuous()` and `scale_y_continuous()`
  can be added to it.
- `scales::comma` writes the axis labels with thousands separators.
:::
:::

The line above the chart is the result of a Pearson correlation test:

| Item | Meaning |
|------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| $t_{\text{Student}}(26) = 3.60$ | test statistic, with 26 degrees of freedom: 28 stores minus 2 |
| $p = 1.32 \times 10^{-3}$ | p-value: the probability of a correlation at least this strong if there were no correlation |
| $\hat{r}_{\text{Pearson}} = 0.58$ | Pearson correlation between the estimated customers and the recorded sales |
| $\text{CI}_{95\%}$ [0.26, 0.78] | 95% confidence interval of the correlation |
| $n_{\text{pairs}} = 28$ | number of stores |

```{r}
#| echo: false
ct2 <- cor.test(store_sales_est$sum_E_j, store_sales_est$Total_Sales)
```

Across the 28 stores, the Pearson correlation between the estimated customers and the recorded sales
is `r round(ct2$estimate, 2)`, with a p-value of `r signif(ct2$p.value, 2)`. A linear fit of the
sales on the estimate explains `r round(100 * ct2$estimate^2)`% of the variation in sales.

The chapter ends with `huff_share_wider`, a table with one column for each store. The table is not
used on this page.

# Part 2: Review and extension

In sections 4.1 to 4.3, the inputs of the Huff model of Part 1 are checked: the study area, the
attraction of the stores and the distance exponent. In sections 4.4 and 4.5, the trade areas and the
estimated sales are compared at the default exponent and at the exponent fitted in section 4.3.

| Section | Task | Source |
|-------|-------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| | **Checks of the chapter's inputs** | |
| 4.1 | Check which parts of Taichung City the villages cover | Wieland (2017), pp. 300, 303; Huff (1963), p. 87 |
| 4.2 | Test the effect of the constant attraction `Store_size = 100` | slide 9; Huff (1963), p. 86; Wieland (2017), p. 299 |
| 4.3 | Fit the distance exponent to the recorded sales of the stores | Huff (1963), pp. 84, 87; Wieland (2017), pp. 299-301; `MCI` manual, `huff.lambda()`, pp. 24-25 |
| | **Results at the fitted exponent** | |
| 4.4 | Map the trade areas as probabilities, at the default and the fitted exponent | Huff (1963), pp. 82, 84, 87; Wieland (2017), p. 298; Rodrigue, A.15 |
| 4.5 | Compare the estimated and recorded sales of each store at the fitted exponent | slide 13; Wieland (2017), p. 300 |

The MCI model of slides 14 and 15 is estimated by regression on observed market shares $p_{ij}$.
Nakanishi and Cooper (1982) showed that the regression can be run with dummy variables in standard
regression packages. Wieland (2017, p. 300) names the MCI model "probably the best way to estimate
the parameters" when $p_{ij}$ is observed. The sales file records the sales of each store by
`POD code`. The `POD code` may record where the customers come from. No table in the data links a
`POD code` to a village, so the share of each village's customers at each store is unknown. The MCI
model is therefore not fitted on this page.

## Study area: unassigned areas and Heping District

Wieland (2017, p. 300) names the first step of a Huff analysis: "to delineate the study area itself
and to record the focused origins and locations". Every origin in the study area receives
probabilities, and an origin outside it has no customers in the model. In chapter 18, the study area
is the villages of `VILLAGE_TC` with a population. The question for this section is which parts of
Taichung City these villages cover.

```{r}
pop_raw <- read_csv("data/aspatial/pop2019.csv") |>
  mutate(V_ID = str_remove_all(V_ID, "-"))

pop_raw |>
  filter(!V_ID %in% village$VILLCODE) |>
  select(V_ID, TOWN, VILLAGE, P_CNT) |>
  kable()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `pop_raw` is a fresh copy of the population table, with the hyphens removed from `V_ID`.
- `filter(!V_ID %in% village$VILLCODE)` keeps the rows of the population table that have no polygon
  in `village`.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
heping <- pop_raw |> filter(!V_ID %in% village$VILLCODE)
port_area <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "VILLAGE_TC", quiet = TRUE) |>
  filter(str_detect(VILLCODE, "S0")) |>
  st_area() |>
  sum() |>
  units::drop_units()
```

The population table has `r nrow(heping)` villages with no polygon, all in Heping District (和平區),
with `r format(sum(heping$P_CNT), big.mark = ",")` residents. The town layer
has `r sum(town$TOWNNAME == "和平區")` polygons named 和平區, so Heping District is missing from the town
layer as well as the village layer. The `r nrow(village)` villages of the study area
cover `r format(round(units::drop_units(sum(st_area(village))) / 1e6), big.mark = ",")` km². The
five unassigned areas removed in section 2.5.4 cover `r round(port_area / 1e6, 1)` km². The
population table lists no residents for them.

Four of the unassigned areas are on the coast of Qingshui, Wuqi and Longjing Districts, and one is
inland in Qingshui District. The map below shows them with the villages of the study area.

::: {.panel-tabset}

The `r format(sum(heping$P_CNT), big.mark = ",")` residents of Heping District
are `r round(100 * sum(heping$P_CNT) / sum(pop_raw$P_CNT), 2)`% of the residents in the population
table. Without a polygon for each of their villages, the distances from these residents to the
stores cannot be computed, so their effect on the estimate of each store is unknown.

Wieland (2017, p. 303) cites the principles of Huff and McCallum (2008) for the study area: "little
in from outside" and "little out from inside", which means "that the majority of shopping
interactions should take place within the study area". The model divides all the residents of
the `r nrow(village)` villages among the 28 stores, so it has no customers from outside the city.
Residents of villages near the city boundary may also use stores in the neighbouring counties, which
are not in the data, so the second principle cannot be checked for these villages.

## Store attraction: constant size versus sales area

Huff (1963, p. 86) measured the attraction of a shopping centre as "the square footage of selling
space devoted to the sale of a particular class of goods". Wieland (2017, p. 299) describes the
attraction as the size of the location, "operationalized by the sales area". In chapter 18, every
store has `Store_size = 100`. The `Capacity` column of `storeCD.csv` is 50 for every store. The
question for this section is what a constant attraction leaves of the Huff model.

```{r}
im_size_1 <- interaction_matrix |>
  mutate(Store_size = 1)
im_size_50 <- interaction_matrix |>
  mutate(Store_size = 50)

p_by_size <- function(huff) {
  huff |>
    arrange(VILLCODE, Store_CD) |>
    pull(p_ij)
}
p_100 <- p_by_size(huff_share)
p_1 <- p_by_size(huff.shares(im_size_1, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
                             "Store_size", "distance"))
p_50 <- p_by_size(huff.shares(im_size_50, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
                              "Store_size", "distance"))

size_diff <- c(size_1_vs_100 = max(abs(p_1 - p_100)),
               size_50_vs_100 = max(abs(p_50 - p_100)))
size_diff
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `im_size_1` and `im_size_50` are copies of the interaction matrix with `Store_size` set to 1 and
  to 50 for every store.
- `huff.shares()` checks its first argument with `exists()`, which looks up the argument by its name
  in the workspace. The function stops with an error when the result of a `|>` chain, or a data
  frame created inside a function, is passed to it. `im_size_1` and `im_size_50` are therefore saved
  under their own names first.
- `p_by_size()` sorts the rows by village and store, so that the probabilities for sizes 1, 50 and
  100 are in the same order, and returns the column `p_ij`. `p_100` holds the probabilities of
  section 3.4.
- `size_diff` holds the largest absolute difference between `p_1` and `p_100`, and between `p_50`
  and `p_100`.
:::

The differences between `p_1` and `p_100` and between `p_50` and `p_100` are below
$10^{`r ceiling(log10(max(size_diff)))`}$, the size of a rounding error. With the same $A_j$ for
every store, $A_j^{\gamma}$ is a common factor of the numerator and the denominator of $p_{ij}$ and
cancels, as in the example of section 3.1. The model of Part 1 is therefore a model of distance
only: a village is divided among the stores by $d_{ij}^{-2}$, and the size of a store has no effect.
The data of the exercise have no sales area, seats or opening hours of the stores. The recorded
sales of the 28 stores differ by a factor
of `r round(max(stores$Total_Sales) / min(stores$Total_Sales), 1)` between the highest and the
lowest (section 2.5.2).

## Distance decay: default exponent versus a fitted exponent

Huff (1963, p. 84) wrote that analysts using the gravity model "have naively assumed that the
exponent 2 which Reilly had originally estimated for intra-urban trade movements would possess the
same value within urban areas". According to Huff, studies had found exponents "from 1.5 to over 3".
In his model, the exponent is "a parameter which is to be estimated empirically" (p. 86). His
estimates were 3.191 for clothing and 2.723 for furniture (p. 87). In chapter 18, the default
`lambda = -2` of `huff.shares()` is used. Wieland (2017, p. 300) writes that "in many cases, no
empirical market shares are available but only observed total sales of stores or locations", and
that many studies therefore fit the Huff model to the observed totals. The data of chapter 18 are of
this kind. The Lesson 8 outline links the `MCI` package, and its reference manual describes
`huff.lambda()` as a function that "estimates a distance decay parameter from observed total
store/location data". According to the manual (p. 25), the fit is "measured using the sum of squared
residuals of observed vs. expected total values".

The question for this section is which value of $\lambda$ gives estimated totals closest to the
recorded sales of the 28 stores. According to Wieland (2017, p. 299), the market area $T_j$ is
"normally measured in persons or money", and the observed and expected totals have to be in the same
unit. The estimated customers are in persons and the sales are in units of money, so the sales are
first rescaled to the same total as the population. The rescaling is valid when the sales of a store
are proportional to its customers.

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_j &= \frac{\text{sales}_j}{\sum_{k=1}^{28} \text{sales}_k} \times \sum_i C_i \\[4pt]
&= \frac{\text{recorded sales of store } j}{\text{recorded sales of all 28 stores}} \times \text{population of all villages}
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r}
D <- st_distance(village_center, stores) |>
  units::drop_units()
P <- village$P_CNT
sales_scaled <- stores$Total_Sales /
  sum(stores$Total_Sales) * sum(P)

huff_total_at <- function(lambda) {
  U <- D^lambda
  p <- U / rowSums(U)
  colSums(p * P)
}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `D` is the distance matrix of section 3.2 without units: `r nrow(village)` rows for the villages
  and 28 columns for the stores.
- `sales_scaled` divides each store's sales by the total sales, and multiplies by the total
  population, so that the 28 values sum to the population.
- `huff_total_at()` computes the Huff model for one value of `lambda` with matrices:
  - `U` holds $d_{ij}^{\lambda}$;
  - `rowSums(U)` gives the sum over the stores of each village;
  - `p` holds the probabilities;
  - `colSums(p * P)` gives the estimated customers $T_j$ of each store.
- The attraction is left out, because a constant attraction cancels (section 4.2).
:::

```{r}
all.equal(unname(huff_total_at(-2)),
          huff_total$sum_E_j[match(stores$Store_CD,
                                   huff_total$suppliers_single)])
```

At `lambda = -2`, the matrix computation gives the same totals as `huff.shares()` and
`shares.total()` in section 3.6.

The values of $\lambda$ from $-0.1$ to $-4$ are tried in steps of 0.1. This search is the "trial and
error" option of `huff.lambda()`, `method = "compare"`, in which "several values are tried and the
best one is found" (`MCI` manual, p. 24). For each value of $\lambda$, the estimated totals
$T_j(\lambda)$ are compared with the rescaled sales $S_j$ by:

- the sum of squared residuals (SSR), the criterion of `huff.lambda()` (`MCI` manual, p. 25);
- the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), formula 6 of Wieland (2017, p. 301), which he lists for
  the overall fit of a Huff model;
- the root mean squared error (RMSE), the SSR converted to persons per store, for the chart of the
  error.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{SSR}(\lambda) &= \sum_{j=1}^{28} \big(T_j(\lambda) - S_j\big)^2 \\
&= \text{sum over the 28 stores of } (\text{estimated customers} - \text{rescaled sales})^2 \\[14pt]
\text{MAPE}(\lambda) &= \frac{100}{28} \sum_{j=1}^{28} \frac{|T_j(\lambda) - S_j|}{S_j} \\[4pt]
&= 100 \times \text{mean over the 28 stores of } \frac{|\text{estimated customers} - \text{rescaled sales}|}{\text{rescaled sales}} \\[14pt]
\text{RMSE}(\lambda) &= \sqrt{\text{SSR}(\lambda) / 28} \\
&= \sqrt{\text{mean over the 28 stores of } (\text{estimated customers} - \text{rescaled sales})^2}
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r}
lambda_fit <- tibble(lambda = seq(-0.1, -4, by = -0.1)) |>
  mutate(est = map(lambda, huff_total_at),
         ssr = map_dbl(est, \(e) sum((e - sales_scaled)^2)),
         mape = map_dbl(est, \(e) 100 * mean(abs(e - sales_scaled) / sales_scaled)),
         r = map_dbl(est, \(e) cor(e, stores$Total_Sales)))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
map(x, f); map_dbl(x, f)                                  # purrr
```

- `lambda` runs from $-0.1$ to $-4$ in steps of 0.1. `map()` computes the 28 totals for each value
  and stores them in the list column `est`.
- For each value, `ssr` is the sum of squared residuals between the estimated and the rescaled
  sales. `mape` is the mean absolute percentage error, and `r` is the Pearson correlation between
  the estimated and the recorded sales.
- `\(e)` is the short form of `function(e)`.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
best <- lambda_fit |> slice_min(ssr, n = 1)
lambda_star <- best$lambda
at2 <- lambda_fit |> filter(abs(lambda + 2) < 1e-9)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Chart

```{r}
#| label: lambda-chart
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.5
p_ssr <- ggplot(lambda_fit, aes(x = lambda, y = sqrt(ssr / 28))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = best, colour = "red", size = 2.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -2, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "lambda", y = "root mean squared error (persons)",
       title = "Error of the estimated store totals") +
  theme_minimal()
p_r <- ggplot(lambda_fit, aes(x = lambda, y = r)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -2, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "lambda", y = "Pearson r with recorded sales",
       title = "Correlation with the recorded sales") +
  theme_minimal()
p_ssr + p_r
```

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: lambda-chart
#| eval: false
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- Each chart draws one line over the 40 values of `lambda`. The dashed line marks the default $-2$
  of the chapter.
- The left chart shows the root mean squared error in persons, the square root of `ssr` divided by
  28, the number of stores. Its lowest point, in red, is at the same `lambda` as the smallest `ssr`.
- `p_ssr + p_r` places the left and the right chart side by side with `patchwork`.
:::
:::

The sum of squared residuals is smallest at $\lambda = `r lambda_star`$, with a mean absolute
percentage error of `r round(best$mape, 1)`%. At the default $\lambda = -2$, the mean absolute
percentage error is `r round(at2$mape, 1)`%. The right chart shows the Pearson correlation of
section 3.6. According to Wieland (2017, p. 300), Huff (1962) estimated $\lambda$ by "comparing
expected and observed market shares by correlation coefficients". The correlation keeps rising as
$\lambda$ approaches 0, the value at which every store receives $1/28$ of every village. A Pearson
correlation does not change when the estimates are shifted or rescaled, so it does not measure how
far the estimates are from the recorded values. The sum of squared residuals measures that distance.
It is the criterion of `huff.lambda()`, which searches for $\lambda$ by bisection:

```{r}
pop_df <- village |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(VILLCODE, P_CNT) |>
  as.data.frame()
obs_df <- data.frame(Store_CD = stores$Store_CD,
                     sales_scaled = sales_scaled)
im_df <- as.data.frame(interaction_matrix)

lambda_bisect <- huff.lambda(im_df, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
                             "Store_size", "distance",
                             lambda_startv = -0.1, lambda_endv = -4,
                             localmarket_dataset = pop_df,
                             origin_id = "VILLCODE", localmarket = "P_CNT",
                             location_dataset = obs_df,
                             location_id = "Store_CD",
                             location_total = "sales_scaled")
lambda_bisect$lambda
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
huff.lambda(huffdataset, origins, locations, attrac, dist,
            lambda_startv, lambda_endv,
            localmarket_dataset, origin_id, localmarket,
            location_dataset, location_id, location_total) # MCI
```

- The first five arguments are those of `huff.shares()`. `lambda_startv` and `lambda_endv` bound the
  search.
- `localmarket_dataset` gives the population of each village, and `location_dataset` gives the
  rescaled sales of each store. `huff.lambda()` computes the Huff totals for trial values of
  $\lambda$, and at each step keeps the half of the search interval with the smaller sum of squared
  residuals. The default number of steps is 10.
- `im_df`, `pop_df` and `obs_df` are saved under their own names as plain data frames. Like
  `huff.shares()`, `huff.lambda()` checks its inputs with `exists()` by name (section 4.2).
:::

`huff.lambda()` returns $\lambda = `r round(lambda_bisect$lambda, 2)`$, close to the
$`r lambda_star`$ of the grid. The fitted exponent is about half the default of the chapter. It is
below the range of 1.5 to over 3 that Huff (1963, p. 84) cites from earlier studies. With a weaker
decay, a store draws more of its customers from distant villages. The distances are straight lines,
where Huff (1963) used travel time. The model lets the 28 stores compete only with each other, and
the data contain no stores of other brands. The sales period is unknown, so a store that opened
during the period has sales for part of it only.

```{r}
#| echo: false
lambda_star <- best$lambda
```

## Trade areas: probability surfaces and the most likely store

The studies reviewed by Huff (1963, pp. 82-84) drew trade areas at the breaking point of Reilly's
law (section 3.1), up to which one city "exercises a dominant trading influence" (p. 82). According
to Huff (p. 84), breaking points convey "an impression that a trading area is a fixed boundary". He
described a retail trade area as "a series of zonal probability contours radiating away from a
shopping center" (p. 87). In "Market Area Analysis", section A.15 of the Methods chapter of *The
Geography of Transport Systems*, Rodrigue describes market areas as "ranges of probabilities that
customers will attend specific locations (Huff's law)". The question for this section is how sharply
the villages are divided among the stores, at the default and the fitted exponent.

```{r}
top_p <- function(lambda) {
  U <- D^lambda
  p <- U / rowSums(U)
  apply(p, 1, max)
}

village <- village |>
  mutate(top_p_2 = top_p(-2),
         top_p_fit = top_p(lambda_star))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
apply(X, MARGIN = 1, FUN = max)                           # base R
```

- `top_p()` computes the probabilities for one value of `lambda`, and `apply(p, 1, max)` returns the
  largest probability of each village, the probability of its most likely store.
- `top_p_2` holds the largest probabilities at the default $-2$, and `top_p_fit` holds the largest
  probabilities at the fitted exponent.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Map

```{r}
#| label: top-p-map
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 6
top_long <- village |>
  select(top_p_2, top_p_fit) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(top_p_2, top_p_fit),
               names_to = "model", values_to = "top_p") |>
  mutate(model = factor(model,
                        levels = c("top_p_2", "top_p_fit"),
                        labels = c("lambda = -2 (chapter)",
                                   paste0("lambda = ", lambda_star, " (fitted)"))))
tm_shape(top_long) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "top_p",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1),
                values = "brewer.yl_gn_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Probability of the\nmost likely store"),
              col = "grey60", lwd = 0.1) +
  tm_facets_wrap(by = "model", ncol = 2) +
tm_shape(stores) +
  tm_dots(fill = "red", size = 0.25) +
  tm_title("Probability of the most likely store, by village") +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 1.5, position = c("right", "top")) +
  tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE, legend.outside = TRUE,
            legend.outside.position = "bottom")
```

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: top-p-map
#| eval: false
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `pivot_longer()` stacks `top_p_2` and `top_p_fit`, so that each village appears twice, once for
  each exponent, with the name of the exponent in `model`.
- `factor()` sets the order of the maps: the default exponent of the chapter first, then the fitted
  exponent.
- `tm_facets_wrap(by = "model")` draws one map for each exponent. The maps for the default and the
  fitted exponent use the same fixed classes, so a colour means the same probability on each map.
:::
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
n_maj_2 <- sum(village$top_p_2 >= 0.5)
n_maj_fit <- sum(village$top_p_fit >= 0.5)
share_in_top <- function(lambda) {
  U <- D^lambda
  p <- U / rowSums(U)
  top <- max.col(p)
  E <- p * P
  sapply(seq_len(ncol(p)), \(j) sum(E[top == j, j]) / sum(E[, j]))
}
in_top_2 <- median(share_in_top(-2))
in_top_fit <- median(share_in_top(lambda_star))
```

At the default exponent, `r n_maj_2` of the `r nrow(village)` villages have a store with a
probability of 0.5 or more. These villages are the dark patches around each store. The median
probability of the most likely store is `r round(median(village$top_p_2), 2)`. At the fitted
exponent, `r n_maj_fit` villages have such a store. The median probability of the most likely store
is `r round(median(village$top_p_fit), 2)`.

A deterministic trade area, in the sense of Wieland (2017, p. 298), is the set of villages where a
store is the most likely store. At the default exponent, the median store
has `r round(100 * in_top_2)`% of its estimated customers in such a trade area. At the fitted
exponent, the share falls to `r round(100 * in_top_fit)`%: most of the estimated customers of a
store live in villages where another store is more likely.

## Store sales: recorded versus estimated at the fitted exponent

On slide 13, the total sales of a store are the sum of its expected customers from each village. In
the algorithm of Wieland (2017, p. 300), the difference between the observed and the expected total
of a store is measured by its absolute percentage error. The question for this section is which
stores the fitted model of section 4.3 overestimates or underestimates.

```{r}
store_fit <- tibble(Store_CD = stores$Store_CD,
                    Store_Name = stores$Store_Name,
                    recorded = sales_scaled,
                    estimated = huff_total_at(lambda_star)) |>
  mutate(ratio = recorded / estimated) |>
  arrange(ratio)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `recorded` holds the rescaled sales of section 4.3, and `estimated` holds the Huff totals at the
  fitted exponent. `recorded` and `estimated` are in persons.
- `ratio` is the recorded value divided by the estimate:
  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \text{ratio}_j &= \frac{S_j}{T_j(\hat{\lambda})} \\[4pt]
  &= \frac{\text{rescaled sales of store } j}{\text{estimated customers of store } j \text{ at the fitted } \lambda}
  \end{aligned}
  $$
  A store with a ratio below 1 sells less than the model estimates, and a store with a ratio above 1
  sells more. The absolute percentage error of Wieland (2017, p. 300) is $|1/\text{ratio}_j - 1|$.
  The ratio is used here because it keeps the direction of the difference.
:::

```{r}
store_fit |>
  slice(c(1:5, (n() - 4):n())) |>
  kable(digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 2),
        format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

The map below shows the ratio of each store.

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: ratio-map
#| eval: false
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `store_ratio` joins the `ratio` of `store_fit` to the store points by `Store_CD`.
- `tm_symbols(fill = "ratio")` colours each store by its class. Red stores sell less than the
  estimate and blue stores sell more. No store has a ratio between 0.56 and 0.8, so the lowest class
  starts at 0.8.
:::
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
low5 <- store_fit |> slice(1:5)
ratio_town <- store_ratio |>
  st_join(select(town, name)) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(ratio)
low5_town <- head(ratio_town, 5)
low5_text <- knitr::combine_words(paste(low5_town$Store_CD, "in", low5_town$name),
                                   oxford_comma = FALSE)
high2_text <- paste(tail(ratio_town$Store_CD, 2), "in", tail(ratio_town$name, 2),
                    collapse = " and ")
```

Stores `r paste(head(low5$Store_CD, -1), collapse = ", ")` and `r tail(low5$Store_CD, 1)` sell
between `r round(100 * min(low5$ratio))`% and `r round(100 * max(low5$ratio))`% of their estimate.
These five stores have the five lowest sales of the 28 stores.
Stores `r paste(tail(store_fit$Store_CD, 2), collapse = " and ")`
sell `r round(100 * (min(tail(store_fit$ratio, 2)) - 1))`%
to `r round(100 * (max(tail(store_fit$ratio, 2)) - 1))`% more than their estimate.

On the map, the five stores with the lowest ratios are in five different districts: `r low5_text`.
The two stores with the highest ratios, `r high2_text`, are neighbours on the west side of the city.

With equal attraction, the estimate of a store depends on its distances to the villages and on their
populations. The data do not record the size or the opening date of a store, so the reason for each
gap cannot be tested here. Under the algorithm of Wieland (2017, p. 300), the gaps would be absorbed
into an adjusted attraction for each store.

# Reflection

In chapter 18, the Huff probabilities of 28 stores are computed for the villages of Taichung City.
The probability map of store BT shows the shape that Huff (1963) described: probabilities that fall
with the distance from the store. The estimated customers of the 28 stores have a Pearson
correlation of $r = `r round(ct2$estimate, 2)`$ with the recorded sales.

**The model of the chapter is a model of distance only.** Every store has the same attraction, so
the attraction cancels from the probabilities, and the result depends on the distances and the
exponent. The data give no sales area or other size variable for the stores.

**The default exponent is not fitted to the data.** Huff (1963) treated the exponent as a parameter
to estimate. Fitted to the recorded sales, the exponent is
about `r abs(round(lambda_bisect$lambda, 1))`, compared with the default of 2. The mean absolute
percentage error of the estimated sales falls from `r round(at2$mape, 1)`%
to `r round(best$mape, 1)`%. The trade areas overlap more at the fitted exponent: the median
probability of the most likely store falls from `r round(median(village$top_p_2), 2)`
to `r round(median(village$top_p_fit), 2)`. The median store has `r round(100 * in_top_fit)`% of its
estimated customers in the villages where it is the most likely store,
against `r round(100 * in_top_2)`% at the default exponent.

**Five stores sell about half of their estimate.** With equal attraction, the estimate of a store
depends on its location. The data contain no sales area, opening date or store type that could
explain the gaps of these stores.

**The study area is the villages with a polygon and a population.** Heping District, which
has `r format(sum(heping$P_CNT), big.mark = ",")` residents, is missing from the boundary layers.
The model divides all the residents of the study area among the 28 stores. It includes no stores of
other brands and no customers from outside the city.

**Limits.** The distances are straight lines from a point in each village, where Huff (1963) used
travel time. The sales period, the meaning of the `POD code` and the opening dates of the stores are
unknown. Without the village of each customer, the MCI model of slides 14 and 15 cannot be estimated
from these data.
